messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] FAFB template for different resolution
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chaoyu,

Thanks for your interest in the natverse. I strongly recommend that you work in physical units (nm or microns) if you are integrating different data. You can rescale any data within R by multiplying the object by an appropriate scaling vector.

Skels.raw=read.neurons(“swcdir”)
Skels=Skels.raw*c(8,8,40,8)

Note the use of a 4-vector to scale the *widths* of the skeletons as well.

You can do the same to convert something in nm to microns.

Skels.um=Skels/rep(1000,4)

The template brain objects like FAFB14 have specific units (nm in that case) and it is not expected that they will be rescaled. However, If you would like to plot associated data like FAFB14.surf you can also rescale them eg.

plot3d(FAFB14.surf/1e3)

To plot in microns rather than nm. From this you will see that at present the natverse does not automatically understand data calibrated in different spatial units, so you need to ensure yourself that data have the same units (nm or microns).

Best wishes,

Greg.

1. The surface object is the “neuropil”. Parts of the neurons (the cell body and cell body fibre, sometimes called primary neurite can be outside)

2. The neuropil surface was constructed by light microscopy and then “bridged” to the em dataset. This has some small inaccuracies.

3. One part of the visual system, the lamina, is not included.

4. The pink thing is not a neuron. I cannot tell if it is a mis-segmentation or perhaps some kind of glia with processes outside the neuropil.

Best,

Greg.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marcel,

This uses Alex Bates' experimental catnat package. from the help for

https://jefferislab.github.io/catnat/reference/catmaid_upload_neurons.html

you can see that you can provide a vector of names, one for each neuron, but the annotations are applied to all neurons.

Assuming that myneuronlist has a column name in the attached dataframe you could do

skids=catmaid_upload_neurons(swc = myneuronlist, name = myneuronlist[,'name'], annotations = ("PFN", "PFN_L", "L7"), pid = 3, conn = server_auth, return.new.skids=TRUE)

Alternatively if you need to apply a different set of annotations to each neuron, you can use catmaid_set_annotations_for_skeletons() on each of the returned neurons.

Best,

Greg.

Dear Zachary,

Thanks for your interest in the natverse tools and sorry you've run into a problem.

Unfortunately the error message is rather generic so it is a bit hard to tell exactly what the problem is, but given your investigations so far, it's unlikely to be the same as the github issue <https://github.com/natverse/nat.templatebrains/issues/38> you found. I think we need to make some small modifications to nat to make this kind of thing easier to debug.

In the meantime, could you go to the terminal and try running

cmtk streamxform <path/to/your/registration.list>

Then type in a space separated triple of plausible 3D coordinates e.g.

100 100 50

Press return and report what happens. One possibility is a partial failure of the install due to missing libraries required to run streamxform but not required for the mat2dof tool. Incidentally depending on how cmtk was installed you sometimes need to do

/usr/lib/cmtk/bin/streamxform <path/to/your/registration.list>

i.e. omitting the leading cmtk (which is a bundled shell script) but ensuring that you either provide the full path to streamxform.

With best wishes,

Greg.

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] Error running CMTK streamxform
messages.body_plain:
Dear Zachary,

I have actually never used CMTK registrations in nii format.

Normally CMTK registrations are distributed in its native format .list since this is the most compact. Occasionally people write deformation fields (essentially an image volume describing the 3D displacement at from target to source for every voxel in the image); these are often in NRRD format. It it certainly possible to write the same field in nii format, but I haven't come across this myself.

At present the nat package only provides support for .list and NRRD format, not nii. However when you tested out your file in the terminal with streamxform, any cmtk supported registration file should have worked. So it doesn't look as if that is what it is.

Most commonly when I have seen a deformation field in .nii format, it has been produce by ANTs software. As it happens the natverse does have some support for that,

https://github.com/jefferis/nat.ants

although it is much less used/tested than other registration formats.

Of course nii format is also commonly used to store regular 3D image values (as opposed to registrations).

Where did your nii file come from?

All the best,

Greg.

Dear Zachary, Yes, I think the Baier lab used ANTs in their most recent work. For info, ANTs and CMTK are independent pieces of software. If this is your first time trying to transform points using registration data, then after installing https://github.com/jefferis/nat.ants#installation read the help file given by

?antsreg

carefully. The directionality of transformations can be a little tricky to get your head round at first. nat follows the CMTK convention which considers the transform required for image data to be the forward transform of any pair, which means the point data will require the inverse transform.

All the best,

Greg.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Zhihao,

I think you should get some specific input from Alex Bates on this, but essentially you will not be able to use flow centrality thresholds that you are used to in FAFB with hemibrain data. As far as I can tell the general reason for this is that many hemibrain neurons have

Most of their axonal output synapses
Most of the inputs onto those axonal arbours (many inputs can be on the shaft or very close to the shaft and are therefore well-recovered).

But proportionally fewer dendritic inputs (mean of ~25% across the brain) and presumably dendritic outputs.

This differential synapse recovery rate will skew some analytics including flow centrality. Of course there will also be some neurons that are truncated etc.

But this does not meant that you can't use flow centrality at all. You just may need to recalibrate.

All the best,

Greg.

Dear George,

Great that you managed to get up and running with Docker.

As for this problem, you actually have 2 versions of CMTK now. One that I compiled from source when making the docker image. That is in /usr/local and another that was downloaded by the Fiji CMTK plugin. The CMTK error that you see below is related to a missing library that the CMTK binaries downloaded by the Fiji CMTK plugin expect to be installed (libdcmdata is related to reading DICOM images).

You should be able to get your scripts to by editing them in a text editor, replacing

-b "/home/george/Fiji.app/bin/cmtk"

with

-b "/usr/local/lib/cmtk/bin"

You can find further details about the error on the CMTK mailing list [1,2], but essentially, it Is necessary to compile CMTK from scratch on recent versions of ubuntu.

Two improvements that I hope to make would be to provide nightly binaries of cmtk built on modern ubuntu version and make the Fiji CMTK use an existing CMTK installation if It can find one [3]. Of course user contributions are very welcome in this area.

All the best,

Greg.

Dear Mike,

Thanks for your message.

1a) You are right, there was a typo in the example, change

ovidns.hemibrain=neuprintr::neuprint_read_neurons('oviDN')

to

ovidns.fib=neuprintr::neuprint_read_neurons('oviDN')

1b) The factor of 8/1000 converts raw voxels to microns and has been covered a couple of times previously on the user group. Please see

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/nat-user/%228$2F1000%22

And let us know if you still have questions.

2. To look at individual neurons, here are some ideas

library(neuprintr)

# WIP package targeted at hemibrain
# see https://github.com/flyconnectome/hemibrainr/
# remotes::install_github("flyconnectome/hemibrainr")
library(hemibrainr)

# this immediately converts to microns
LPLC4=hemibrain_read_neurons("LPLC4", microns=TRUE)

# clear 3D display
nclear3d()
# brain surface for context
plot3d(hemibrainr::hemibrain_microns.surf, alpha=.2)
# plot all
plot3d(LPLC4, soma=T)

# just one, chosen by position in the results list
nclear3d()
plot3d(hemibrainr::hemibrain_microns.surf, alpha=.2)
plot3d(LPLC4[1], soma=T)

# chosen by bodyid
nclear3d()
plot3d(hemibrainr::hemibrain_microns.surf, alpha=.2)
plot3d(LPLC4["5812990157"], soma=T)

# scan through neurons one by one
nclear3d()
plot3d(hemibrainr::hemibrain_microns.surf, alpha=.2)
nlscan(LPLC4, soma=T, lwd=2)

3. Please feel free to keep asking questions here, but as mentioned at http://natverse.org/learn/, we recommend working through

http://natverse.org/nat/articles/neurons-intro.html

And scanning

http://natverse.org/nat/reference/

This will probably save you time in the long run.

All the best,

Greg.

Dear Isabel,

There is of course a way to do this – and we have been doing so for internal use for a while now. In theory, you can just download the SWC files en masse by following the link from the hemibrain website to the DVID blog, convert them to the right template space (as described earlier in this thread) and then to dotprops format.

There are some wrinkles though as you need to decide which template space to use for your calculations (it needs to be calibrated in microns). We have also found that some preprocessing is necessary to remove numerous small twigs, especially when comparing light level neurons with EM neurons. Otherwise the twigs dominate the score over the neuronal backbone. We normally use twig thresholds of 2-5 µm.

http://natverse.org/nat/reference/prune_twigs.html

We have not distributed NBLAST ready versions of all the skeletons because FlyEM should soon be releasing their own. However if you want to know more in the interim, feel free to contact me off list.

All the best,

Greg.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Isabel,

If you want to make a more dilated volumetric rendition of a neuron, you can either

* increase the voxel size (by making an object with the same bounding box as JRC2018U) but larger voxels

* do some appropriate 3D convolution on the line object.

The natverse is not particularly set up for the latter, but I have used Fiji/ImageJ for this purpose after writing out a nrrd file as you have done below. You could use e.g. the Gaussian 3D operation with a 2 µm kernel.

When I had a lot of this work to do, I have also used the unu command line tool [1] resample command to do the filtering. There are a a range of alternatives to the gaussian kernel which may be better in retaining the sparse nature of the dataset. One other thing, it is important to save compressed nrrds (e.g. gz) for this kind of work since the image volumes will only have a few non-zero pixels.

All the best,

Greg.

[1] http://teem.sourceforge.net/unrrdu/
